newsitem.title: USA: Melting snow forms vast lake in northern U.S. plains.
newsitem.headline: Melting snow forms vast lake in northern U.S. plains.

text.p: Melting snow created vast lakes in the Red River Valley at the Canadian-U.S. border on Friday, endangering rural communities and forcing evacuations, authorities said.
Hundreds of homes were surrounded by the icy waters, and low-lying farmland was covered by runoff from the heaviest winter snowfall ever recorded.

"We have severe overland flooding," North Dakota State University geologist Donald Schwert said in Fargo, which sits in the centre of the 50-mile (80 km) -wide Red River Valley that extends like a table-top into Canada.

"The snow has been transformed into water and is turning vast areas into lakes, covering tens of square miles. It's flowing over fields, endangering rural communities and making its way to the Red River Valley," he said.
Adding to the spring miseries was another storm that brought rain and heavy, wet snow to the hard-hit Dakotas and Minnesota.
"The conditions are bad enough the way they are. The river models at some locations will exceed record levels -- even without the rain," National Weather Service hydrologist Wendy Pearson said.
No deaths or serious injuries had been reported since a woman and her teenage daughter died after plunging off a washed-out road with their horse trailer on Monday night.

Several tributaries of the north-flowing Red River had already reached record crests, blocking roads and swamping small towns such as Casselton, La Moure, and Milnor. Dozens of people had to be evacuated, some by four-wheel-drive vehicles, others by boat.
Backhoes and farm machinery were employed to break up ice and snowdrifts blocking culverts and ravines so that floodwaters could flow away from homes.
Volunteers rushed to finish sandbag walls and temporary dikes in Fargo, while massive pumps were moved into position to deal with the rising waters.

With the melting process moving gradually north, National Guard helicopters made repeated runs over the iced-over Red River, sprinkling sand on the ice to try to speed up the melt and prevent ice-jams.

"The rain and snow will only make things muddy, wet and sloppy and add to groundwater problems. The last thing people need is more snow," said Capt. Pat Richards of North Dakota's Division of Emergency Management.
